try.es: Pruébalo en la caja de ritmos

lessons.title: Why a Steady Pulse Helps
lessons.mainIdea: People naturally sync their movements to a steady beat, and a predictable pulse can help the body and brain settle and focus.
reading: Put on a song and watch a room. Heads nod, feet tap, and often nobody decided to do it. Moving in time with a beat is called *synchronizing*. People do it from a young age, and it gets stronger with practice. Rowers pull together. Marchers step together. Dancers at the Warehouse moved together.

Scientists who study the brain find that hearing a steady beat activates areas that plan movement, even when you sit still. The brain starts to predict when the next beat will come. When it guesses right, that can feel satisfying. That may be part of why a steady pulse feels good.

A steady pulse can also be a tool. Some people focus better with a quiet, steady beat in their headphones. Some people rock, tap or bounce a knee to think. That movement is the body finding its own rhythm, and it can help. Therapists use rhythm to help people walk more evenly after an injury and to practice speech. A beat is something the body understands.

words.d: to move or happen at the same time as something else
to say what will happen next based on a pattern

look.title: The Walking Beat
look.text: A physical therapist plays a steady click at a comfortable walking pace. A patient learning to walk again after an injury tries to step on each click. Over several weeks, her steps become more even.
look.prompt: Why might a steady beat make stepping easier? What does the brain get from the click?

check.q: What does it mean to synchronize with a beat?
choices: To stop moving when the beat starts
To move at the same time as the beat
check.why: Synchronizing means lining your movement up with the pulse.

check.q: Why might a steady beat feel satisfying?
choices: The beat makes the room warmer
The beat blocks all other sounds
The brain predicts the next beat and gets it right
The ear only hears steady sounds
check.why: The brain enjoys a pattern it can predict.

check.q: A student bounces a knee while solving a problem. What is a helpful way to see this?
choices: The body is finding a rhythm that can help thinking
It means the student is not paying attention
It always shows the student is upset
It stops the brain from working
check.why: Many people think better with movement. A steady rhythm can help focus.

lessons.title: Rhythms in Nature
lessons.mainIdea: Nature is full of rhythms that can be measured, and some of them change in a predictable way.
reading: Beats are not only made by people. Crickets chirp in rhythm. Frogs call in turns. Fireflies in some places flash together. Your heart keeps its own tempo, faster when you run, slower when you rest. These are *natural rhythms*.

In 1897, a physics teacher named Amos Dolbear wrote about crickets. He noticed that crickets chirp faster when the air is warmer and slower when it is cooler. A cricket's body warms and cools with the air, so its muscles work faster in the heat. Dolbear turned the chirp rate into a way to estimate temperature.

Scientists still use this idea. The chirp tempo is a *variable* that changes along with another variable, temperature. When two things change together in a steady way, you can use one to predict the other. You will do the same with your own beats in Chapter 64.

words.d: a repeating pattern in nature, like a heartbeat or a cricket's chirp
something that can change or be changed in an investigation

look.title: The Cricket Thermometer
look.text: Dolbear wrote that the rate of a cricket's chirp depends on the temperature, and gave a rule for finding the temperature by counting chirps for one minute.
look.cite: Amos Dolbear, The Cricket as a Thermometer, The American Naturalist, 1897
look.prompt: What two variables did Dolbear connect? How could you check his idea on a summer night?

check.q: What did Dolbear notice about crickets?
choices: They chirp faster when it is cooler
They chirp faster when it is warmer
check.why: Warmer air lets the cricket's muscles work faster, so it chirps faster.

check.q: Which is a natural rhythm?
check.why: A heartbeat is a repeating pattern made by the body, not by a machine.

check.q: Your heart rate is higher after running. What changed?
choices: Your heart stopped having a beat
The tempo of your heartbeat went up
The pitch of your heart changed
Your heartbeat became a wave in the air
check.why: Running speeds up your heart, a higher tempo.

lessons.title: When a Beat Becomes a Note
lessons.mainIdea: A click repeated faster than about 20 times a second stops sounding like a rhythm and starts sounding like a pitch.
reading: Here is a strange fact that joins this chapter to the last one. Take a single click and repeat it 4 times a second. You hear a fast rhythm. Repeat it 10 times a second and it becomes a buzz of clicks. Repeat it more than about 20 times a second, and your brain stops hearing separate clicks. You hear a low tone.

Why? A click repeated 100 times a second is a vibration at 100 Hz. That is a frequency, and frequency is pitch. The difference between a rhythm and a note is only speed. Rhythm lives at slow repetition rates. Pitch lives at fast ones. The *threshold* between them sits around 20 per second.

So a beat at 120 BPM is a very slow vibration, 2 per second. A bass note at 110 Hz is the same idea sped up 55 times. Musicians and scientists both work with repeating patterns in time. They just work at different speeds.

words.d: the point where one thing changes into another
how many vibrations or waves happen each second

look.title: Speeding Up the Click
look.text: A computer plays a click once per second, then 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100 times per second. Listeners say when it stops sounding like clicks.
look.prompt: Around what rate do you predict listeners will hear a tone? What pitch would 100 clicks per second make?

check.q: A click repeats 100 times a second. What do you hear?
choices: A low tone at about 100 Hz
check.why: Above about 20 per second, repeats blend into a pitch.

check.q: What is the only real difference between a rhythm and a pitch?
check.why: Slow repeats sound like rhythm, fast repeats sound like pitch.

check.q: A beat is at 120 BPM. How many times per second does it repeat?
check.why: 120 beats divided by 60 seconds is 2 per second.

review.q: What is a beat?
choices: An event that repeats at an even spacing in time
review.why: A beat repeats evenly, like a clock tick.

review.q: What unit measures tempo?
review.why: Tempo is counted in BPM.

review.q: At 60 BPM, how long does each beat last?
review.why: 60 seconds divided by 60 beats is one second each.

review.q: A 16-step bar in 4/4 gives each beat how many steps?
review.why: 16 steps divided by 4 beats is 4 steps per beat.

review.q: Kick on 1 and 9, snare on 5 and 13. On which beats is the snare?
review.why: Steps 5 and 13 are beats two and four.

review.q: What does swing change?
choices: The timing of every second step
review.why: Swing plays every second step a little late.

review.q: A cricket chirps faster. According to Dolbear, what likely changed?
review.why: Chirp rate rises with temperature.

review.q: Clicks repeat 200 times a second. What do you hear?
choices: A slow beat you can dance to
review.why: Fast repeats blend into pitch.

chapters.title: Recording and Playing Back
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a sound, which is gone in a moment, be caught and played again years later?

story.title: Mary Had a Little Lamb
story.kicker: In 1877, Thomas Edison spoke into a machine, and the machine spoke back.
paragraphs: In December 1877, in his laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey, Thomas Edison tried a new machine. It had a metal cylinder wrapped in a thin sheet of tinfoil, a crank to turn it, and a mouthpiece with a small needle attached behind a thin plate.

Edison turned the crank and shouted into the mouthpiece. As his voice shook the plate, the needle pressed a wobbly track into the foil. Then he moved the needle back to the start and turned the crank again. Out came a thin, scratchy voice: Mary had a little lamb.

People had never heard anything like it. Before this, a sound was gone the moment it ended. A voice could be remembered, but not kept. Now a voice could be pressed into a surface and played back. The machine was called the phonograph, which means sound writer.

Every record on the Turntables and every sound in the Drum Machine comes from that idea: turn the shape of a sound wave into something that lasts. In this chapter you will follow that idea from wobbly grooves to lists of numbers.
story.think: Edison's needle pressed a track into foil. What do you think the shape of that track had to do with his voice?

lessons.title: The First Machines That Kept Sound
lessons.mainIdea: The first recording machines turned the vibrations of sound into a line traced on a surface.
reading: Twenty years before Edison, a French printer named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville built the *phonautograph*. Sound shook a thin skin, and a bristle attached to it traced a wavy line on paper blackened with soot. It could write sound down, but it could not play it back.

Edison's *phonograph* of 1877 could do both. The needle pressed the wave into tinfoil. Running the needle back over the track made it shake the same way again. The shaking plate pushed the air, and the sound came back out. For the first time, a recording could be heard.

In 2008, researchers scanned some of Scott's old paper tracings and used computers to turn the lines back into sound. One of them, from 1860, is a person singing a few notes of the French song Au clair de la lune. It is one of the oldest recordings of a human voice we can hear today.

words.d: an 1850s machine that traced sound waves as lines on paper but could not play them back
Edison's 1877 machine that recorded sound as a track and played it back

look.title: A Machine That Talks
look.text: Edison wrote that the phonograph could keep a voice, a lesson or a piece of music exactly, so it could be heard again whenever wanted, even after the speaker had died.
look.cite: Thomas A. Edison, The Phonograph and Its Future, North American Review, 1878
look.prompt: What uses did Edison imagine? Which ones came true?

check.q: What could the phonautograph not do?
check.why: It wrote sound waves on paper but had no way to turn them back into sound.

check.q: What did Edison's phonograph add?
check.why: The phonograph could both record and play back.

check.q: How were Scott's 1860 tracings finally heard?
choices: Edison played them on his phonograph
They were always on a record
Researchers scanned them and turned the lines into sound with computers
check.why: Computers read the traced wave shape and rebuilt the sound in 2008.

lessons.title: A Groove Is a Wave You Can Touch
lessons.mainIdea: A record's groove is a long spiral whose tiny side-to-side wiggles copy the shape of the sound wave.
reading: Look at a vinyl record in bright light. You see fine rings. It is actually one very long *groove* that spirals from the outside edge toward the center. Under a microscope, the groove is not smooth. Its walls wiggle from side to side.

Those wiggles are the sound wave, frozen in plastic. A slow, wide wiggle is a low, loud note. A quick, tiny wiggle is a high, soft note. When the record spins, a tiny tip called the *stylus* rides in the groove. The wiggles push it back and forth, the same way the air pushed the microphone.

The stylus is joined to a *cartridge*, which turns its movement into a small electrical signal. An amplifier makes the signal stronger, and a speaker cone moves with it, pushing the air. The wiggle in the plastic has become a wave in the air again. A stereo record even carries two signals, one on each wall of the groove, for the left and right speakers.

words.d: the long spiral track cut into a record whose wiggles hold the sound wave
the tiny tip, often diamond, that rides in a record's groove
the part of a turntable that turns the stylus's movement into an electrical signal

look.title: Following the Groove
look.text: A student looks at a record under a magnifier. In one spot the groove wiggles in wide, slow curves. In another spot the wiggles are tiny and packed close together.
look.prompt: Which spot probably holds a low bass note? Which holds a high sound? Explain using frequency.

check.q: What do the wiggles in a record's groove hold?
choices: The shape of the sound wave
check.why: The side-to-side wiggles copy the sound wave's pattern.

check.q: What does the stylus do?
choices: Rides in the groove and moves with its wiggles
check.why: The stylus follows the wiggles, turning them back into motion.

check.q: Quick, tiny wiggles close together most likely hold what kind of sound?
check.why: Close wiggles mean high frequency. Small wiggles mean small amplitude.

lessons.title: Speed Matters
lessons.mainIdea: A record must spin at the speed it was made for; faster raises the pitch and tempo, slower lowers them.
reading: Records are made to spin at a set speed, counted in revolutions per minute, or *rpm*. Long-playing albums spin at 33 and one third rpm. Seven-inch singles often spin at 45 rpm. Old shellac records from before about 1950 spin near 78 rpm.

Play a record at the wrong speed and something odd happens. Play a 33 record at 45, and the voices sound high and chipmunky, and the song rushes. Play a 45 at 33, and the voices drop low and slow. The wiggles pass the stylus faster or slower, so every *frequency* and the whole tempo change together.

The math is neat. 45 divided by 33 and one third is 1.35. Every frequency goes up by 35 percent, and the BPM goes up by the same amount. A 100 BPM song becomes a 135 BPM song. On the Turntables you can switch speeds and hear this for yourself.

words.d: revolutions per minute: how many full turns something makes in one minute
how many vibrations or waves happen each second

look.title: Record Speeds
look.cite: Standard record speeds; 33 and one third rpm shown as 33.3
look.prompt: How many times faster is 78 rpm than 33 and one third rpm? What would a voice sound like if an LP were played at 78?

check.q: A 33 rpm record is played at 45 rpm. What happens?
choices: Pitch and tempo both go up
check.why: The wiggles pass faster, raising every frequency and the tempo together.

check.q: What does rpm stand for?
check.why: rpm counts full turns each minute.

check.q: A 100 BPM song on a 33 record is played at 45 rpm. About what BPM do you hear?
check.why: 45 divided by 33 and one third is 1.35, so 100 becomes about 135.

lessons.title: Scratching
lessons.mainIdea: Scratching is moving a record back and forth by hand, which plays a slice of the recording forward and backward.
reading: In the mid-1970s in the Bronx, in New York City, DJs were inventing hip hop at block parties. One teenager, Grand Wizzard Theodore, is often credited with making scratching into a technique. He stopped a spinning record with his hand, moved it back and forth under the needle, and liked the sound.

Here is the science. When your hand pushes the record forward, the stylus reads the groove forward, and you hear the sound. Pull it back and the stylus reads the groove backward, so the sound plays in reverse. How fast you move your hand sets the *playback speed*, and that sets the pitch. A fast push gives a high zip. A slow drag gives a low growl.

A scratch is really a performance of physics. Your hand becomes the motor. You are choosing, moment by moment, how fast and in which direction the recording plays. DJs combine this with a *crossfader*, a slider that cuts the sound in and out, to make rhythms on top of the beat.

words.d: moving a record back and forth under the needle by hand to make rhythmic sounds
how fast a recording is played compared to how it was recorded
a slider on a DJ mixer that fades between two sound sources or cuts one in and out

look.title: Push, Pull, Pause
look.text: A DJ holds a record still, pushes it forward quickly for a quarter turn, then drags it back slowly to where it started.
look.prompt: Describe what you would hear on the push and on the pull. Why do they sound different?

check.q: What happens when a DJ pulls a record backward?
check.why: The stylus reads the groove backward, so the recording plays in reverse.

check.q: A DJ moves the record very fast. What happens to the pitch?
check.why: Faster playback raises every frequency.

check.q: Where did scratching begin?
choices: At hip hop parties in the Bronx in the 1970s
check.why: Scratching grew out of Bronx block parties in the mid-1970s.

lessons.title: Pitch Up, Pitch Down
lessons.mainIdea: A pitch control changes a turntable's speed a little, so a DJ can make two records play at the same tempo.
reading: Most DJ turntables have a slider called a *pitch control*. It speeds the platter up or slows it down by a few percent. On many classic turntables, the range is about 8 percent up or down. A record at 120 BPM can be nudged to about 110 or about 130.

Because a record plays pitch and tempo together, speeding it up raises its pitch slightly too. Over a small range, most listeners barely notice. Over a big range, voices start to sound strange. Many digital tools today can change tempo without changing pitch. A turntable cannot. Its sound is tied to its speed.

Why would a DJ want to change the speed at all? Two songs are rarely the same tempo. To blend them smoothly, the DJ has to make them match. That is the next lesson. The pitch slider is the tool, and your ears are the measuring instrument.

words.d: a slider that changes a turntable's speed by a small percentage
a part out of 100; 8 percent of 120 is about 10

look.title: Matching the Numbers
look.text: Record A plays at 124 BPM. Record B plays at 120 BPM. The DJ wants B to match A.
look.prompt: Should the DJ speed B up or slow it down? By about how many percent? What will happen to B's pitch?

check.q: What does a turntable's pitch control change?
check.why: The pitch slider changes how fast the record spins.

check.q: A record at 120 BPM is sped up by 5 percent. What is the new tempo?
check.why: 5 percent of 120 is 6, so the tempo becomes 126.

check.q: On a turntable, what else changes when you speed up a record?
choices: The pitch goes up a little
check.why: A turntable ties pitch to speed.

lessons.title: Blending Two Records
lessons.mainIdea: Beatmatching lines up two records so their beats fall together, letting a DJ move from one song to the next without a bump.
reading: When a DJ blends two records, both play at once for a while. If their beats do not line up, the kicks clatter like two people walking out of step. Lining them up is called *beatmatching*. It needs two things: the same tempo, and beats that land at the same moment.

First the DJ matches tempo with the pitch control, listening in headphones to the new record while the old one plays for the crowd. Then the DJ lines up the *downbeat*, the first beat of a bar, often by giving the new record a small push or drag by hand. If the beats slowly drift apart, the tempos are still a little off.

This is a real measurement task, done by ear. The DJ compares two rhythms, notices drift, adjusts one variable, and checks again. Scientists do the same when they calibrate an instrument. The Turntables let you try it with two decks and a crossfader.

words.d: adjusting two records so their tempos match and their beats land together
the first beat of a bar, the one

look.title: Drifting Apart
look.text: A DJ starts two records together, kick on kick. At first they match. After eight bars, the new record's kick is landing just before the old record's kick.
look.prompt: Which record is faster? What should the DJ do with the pitch control?

check.q: What is beatmatching?
choices: Playing two songs in different keys
Making two records' beats line up in time
Matching the colors of two records
check.why: Beatmatching lines up tempo and beat position.

check.q: Two records slowly drift apart. What does that tell the DJ?
choices: The tempos are not quite equal
check.why: Drift means one record is a little faster than the other.

check.q: What is the downbeat?
choices: The first beat of a bar
The last beat of a song
check.why: The downbeat is the one, the start of each bar.

lessons.title: Sampling: Measuring Many Times a Second
lessons.mainIdea: Digital recording measures a sound wave thousands of times each second and stores each measurement as a number.
reading: A record stores sound as a continuous wiggle. A computer cannot store a wiggle. It stores numbers. So digital recording measures the height of the sound wave again and again, very quickly. Each measurement is a *sample*. The list of samples is the recording.

How often you measure is the *sample rate*, counted in samples per second, or hertz. A music CD takes 44,100 samples every second. That sounds like a lot, and it is. Measuring often matters because a wave that wiggles fast needs many measurements to catch its shape.

There is a rule for this. To record a frequency, you must sample more than twice as fast as that frequency. So a sample rate of 44,100 Hz can capture sounds up to about 22,000 Hz, just above the top of human hearing. That is why the CD rate was chosen. A slower sample rate loses the highest sounds.

words.d: one measurement of a sound wave's height at a single moment
how many samples are taken each second, measured in hertz

look.title: Samples Every Second
look.prompt: Which one can record the highest sounds? About what is the highest frequency the 1987 drum machine can store?

check.q: What is a sample in digital sound?
choices: A piece of a vinyl groove
One measurement of the wave's height
check.why: Each sample is one number measuring the wave at one moment.

check.q: A CD's sample rate is 44,100 Hz. About what is the highest sound it can store?
check.why: You can capture up to about half the sample rate.

check.q: Why must the sample rate be high to record high sounds?
choices: Fast wiggles need many measurements to catch their shape
check.why: You must sample more than twice as fast as the wave wiggles.

lessons.title: Bit Depth: How Fine the Ruler Is
lessons.mainIdea: Bit depth sets how many different heights each sample can have; more bits means finer detail and less hiss.
reading: Each sample is a measurement of height. But how exact is it? Imagine measuring with a ruler marked only in whole inches, versus one marked in tiny millimeters. The finer ruler gives more exact answers. In digital sound, the fineness of the ruler is the *bit depth*.

A *bit* is a single 0 or 1. With more bits, you can write more different numbers. Each extra bit doubles the count. 8 bits can store 256 different heights. 12 bits can store 4,096. 16 bits, used on CDs, can store 65,536.

When the ruler is rough, each sample gets rounded to the nearest mark. That rounding adds a faint hiss or grit to the sound, called *quantization noise*. More bits means smaller rounding and a cleaner sound. Fewer bits means a rougher, crunchier sound, which some musicians love on purpose.

words.d: a single 0 or 1, the smallest piece of computer information
how many bits each sample uses, which sets how many different heights it can store
the faint hiss or grit added when samples are rounded to the nearest level

look.title: How Many Heights Each Sample Can Have
look.cite: Worked out as 2 raised to the number of bits
look.prompt: How many times more levels does 16-bit have than 12-bit? Why might 12-bit sound grittier?

check.q: What does bit depth control?
choices: How many different heights each sample can have
check.why: Bit depth is the fineness of the measuring ruler.

check.q: How many levels can 12 bits store?
check.why: 2 multiplied by itself 12 times is 4,096.

check.q: Fewer bits add what to the sound?
choices: More grit or hiss from rounding
check.why: Rougher rounding adds quantization noise.

lessons.title: The Crunch of a 1987 Sampler
lessons.mainIdea: A famous 1987 sampling drum machine used 12 bits at 26.04 kHz, and its limits gave its drums a gritty sound that shaped hip hop.
reading: In 1987, a sampling drum machine came out that would become a legend. It could record short sounds, like a drum hit from an old record, and play them back on its pads in a sequence. Its sample rate was 26,040 samples per second. Its bit depth was 12 bits.

Those numbers had *limits*. At 26,040 Hz, the highest sound it could store was about 13,000 Hz, so the sparkly top of the cymbals was cut off. At 12 bits, each sample had 4,096 levels, so there was a little grit. Producers also sped samples up to fit more into its short memory, then slowed them down on playback, which added even more crunch.

Hip hop producers in New York loved that sound. It made drums feel heavy, warm and a little rough. Many producers still add grit on purpose to copy it. The Drum Machine on this site copies that 1987 recipe, 12 bits at 26.04 kHz. A limit in a tool became a style. That happens a lot in the history of technology.

words.d: the edge of what a tool can do
a machine that records short sounds and plays them back, often on pads or keys

look.title: Good Enough or Better Than Perfect?
look.text: A producer has two versions of the same drum loop. One is recorded at 16-bit, 44.1 kHz. The other goes through a 12-bit, 26.04 kHz sampler. The second one sounds duller at the very top and a little gritty. The producer picks the second one.
look.prompt: What was lost in the second version? Why might the producer still choose it?

check.q: What was the 1987 sampler's sample rate?
check.why: It sampled at 26.04 kHz.

check.q: About what is the highest sound that sampler could store?
check.why: Half of 26,040 is about 13,000.

check.q: Why did the sampler's limits become a style?
choices: The limits made it louder than any other machine
It was the only machine allowed
Producers liked the heavy, gritty sound they made
check.why: The grit and dull top gave drums a sound people loved and still copy.

try.en: Try it on the Drum Machine
try.es: Pruébalo en la caja de ritmos

lessons.title: Analog and Digital Side by Side
lessons.mainIdea: Analog recording stores a continuous copy of the wave; digital recording stores a list of numbers, and each way has strengths.
reading: A record groove is an *analog* recording. Analog means the stored shape changes smoothly, just like the wave itself. A tape recording is analog too. Every tiny change in the wave becomes a tiny change in the groove or the tape.

A CD, a phone recording and a drum machine sample are *digital*. Digital means the wave is stored as a list of separate numbers. Between samples there is no information, but with enough samples and enough bits, your ear cannot tell the difference.

Each way has strengths. Digital copies are exact; copy a file a thousand times and it does not change. Analog records wear a little each time the stylus rides the groove, and dust adds pops. But a record can be scratched by hand, slowed by a finger and felt in a way a file cannot. Many DJs today use both: digital files controlled with special records that act like analog ones.

words.d: stored as a smooth, continuous copy of the original wave
stored as a list of separate numbers

look.title: Copy of a Copy
look.text: A band records a song. Version 1 is copied from tape to tape ten times. Version 2 is a digital file copied from computer to computer ten times.
look.prompt: Which version will sound more like the original after ten copies? Why?

check.q: Which is an analog recording?
choices: A music file on a phone
check.why: A record groove is a smooth, continuous copy of the wave.

check.q: What is one strength of digital recording?
choices: It can be scratched by hand
Copies are exact and do not wear out
It has no numbers in it
check.why: A digital file is the same list of numbers every time it is copied.

check.q: Why can a record get noisier over time?
choices: The stylus and dust wear the groove a little
check.why: Physical wear and dust add pops and hiss to analog records.

review.q: What did Edison's phonograph do that the phonautograph could not?
review.why: The phonograph both recorded and played back.

review.q: What in a record's groove holds the sound?
review.why: The wiggles copy the sound wave.

review.q: A record plays faster than it should. What happens?
review.why: Faster playback raises all frequencies and the tempo.

review.q: In scratching, what sets the pitch of the sound?
choices: How fast the hand moves the record
How hard the button is pressed
review.why: Faster hand movement plays the groove faster, raising the pitch.

review.q: What is beatmatching?
choices: Choosing two songs with the same name
Counting the grooves on a record
Lining up two records' tempos and beats
review.why: Beatmatching makes two records play in step.

review.q: A sample rate of 26,040 Hz can store sounds up to about what?
review.why: The limit is about half the sample rate.

review.q: How many levels can 16 bits store?
review.why: 2 raised to the 16th power is 65,536.

review.q: Which statement about analog and digital is true?
choices: Digital files wear out when played
Digital copies stay exact; analog records can wear
review.why: Digital files copy exactly, while grooves wear with use.

chapters.title: Making It Your Own
chapters.bigQuestion: How can you design a beat for a purpose, then use measurements to show it does what you planned?

story.title: A First Beat, Measured
story.kicker: Jada wanted a beat to help her class settle after lunch. Then she wanted proof it worked.
paragraphs: Jada's class came back from lunch loud and bouncy every day. Her teacher asked the class to design something to help everyone settle into reading time. Jada had one idea right away: a beat. A calm one, low and steady, that the class could breathe along with.

She opened the Drum Machine and set the tempo to 70 BPM, a little slower than a resting heart. She put a soft kick on the first beat of each bar and a quiet hi-hat on the off steps. No crash cymbals. No sudden sounds. She played it for her table. Two friends said it was too sleepy. One said it helped.

Jada wanted more than opinions. She played the beat into the Oscilloscope and looked at it. The kick drew slow, rounded waves. The hi-hat drew thin, fuzzy spikes. She checked that the loudest part was not too tall. She counted the time between kicks on the screen and got about 3.4 seconds, one full bar at 70 BPM.

Then she tested it. For one week the class heard her beat after lunch. For another week they did not. Each day, the teacher timed how long it took for the room to be ready to read. Jada had a claim, a plan and a way to measure. In this chapter, you will design and test a beat of your own.
story.think: What made Jada's project an investigation and not just a song? Name the parts.

lessons.title: Start With a Purpose
lessons.mainIdea: Good design starts with a clear purpose and a list of what the design must do.
reading: Engineers do not start by building. They start with a question: what is this for? Jada's purpose was to help a class settle. Another student might want a beat for a dance, for a workout, or for walking the dog. The purpose shapes every choice.

Next come the *criteria*, the things the design must do to succeed. For a calm beat, the criteria might be: slow tempo, steady pulse, no sudden loud sounds. Then come the *constraints*, the limits you must work within. Maybe you have only 16 steps, one bar, and five minutes.

Writing these down first saves time later. When you are not sure whether to add a crash cymbal, check the criteria. No sudden loud sounds? Then leave it out. Criteria also tell you what to measure when you test. Design and science meet here: a clear goal leads to a fair test.

words.d: the things a design must do to be a success
the limits a design must work within, such as time, tools or space

look.title: Two Purposes
look.text: Student A wants a beat for a school dance. Student B wants a beat to help people focus while reading.
look.prompt: Write two criteria for each beat. How are they different? What tempo might each one use?

check.q: What should a design start with?
check.why: Knowing the purpose shapes every choice.

check.q: Which is a criterion for a calm beat?
choices: Only one bar of steps allowed
Must be done in five minutes
Must be made on a Tuesday
check.why: Criteria describe success. The others are constraints or not relevant.

check.q: Having only 16 steps is an example of what?
check.why: A constraint is a limit you work within.

lessons.title: Build in Layers
lessons.mainIdea: Building a beat one layer at a time lets you hear what each part adds.
reading: Most producers build a beat in *layers*. Start with the kick drum alone and get it feeling right. Then add the snare. Listen. Then add the hi-hat. Listen again. Each layer should earn its place.

Building in layers is like adding one ingredient at a time when you cook. If the soup tastes wrong, you know what changed. If you add everything at once and it sounds messy, it is hard to tell which part is the problem. This is also how scientists build a *model*: start simple, then add parts.

Leaving space is part of the design too. A step with no sound is called a *rest*. Rests give the beat room to breathe, and they make the sounds around them stand out. A beat with every step filled can feel crowded. For many people, a beat with space in it is easier to listen to and to move with.

words.d: one part of a beat, such as the kick or the hi-hat, added on top of the others
a step or moment in music with no sound
a simple version of something that helps us understand or test it

look.title: Too Busy
look.text: A student fills every one of the 16 steps with a kick, a snare and a hi-hat all at once. Friends say it sounds like a washing machine.
look.prompt: What would you tell the student to try? Which layer would you start with and why?

check.q: Why build a beat one layer at a time?
choices: So you can hear what each part adds
So the beat is always faster
Because the machine only has one sound
check.why: Adding one layer at a time shows the effect of each part.

check.q: What is a rest in music?
choices: A step or moment with no sound
check.why: A rest is silence, and it gives the beat space.

check.q: A beat sounds messy. What does building in layers help you do?
choices: Find which part causes the problem
check.why: When you add one part at a time, you know what changed.

try.en: Try it on the Drum Machine
try.es: Pruébalo en la caja de ritmos

lessons.title: Change One Thing at a Time
lessons.mainIdea: To learn what a change does, change only one variable and keep everything else the same.
reading: Say your beat feels too rushed. You could change the tempo, move the snare, and turn off the hi-hat all at once. If it gets better, which change helped? You cannot tell. Change one thing at a time.

The thing you change on purpose is the *independent variable*. What you watch for is the *dependent variable*. Everything else you keep the same is a *controlled variable*. If you change the tempo from 90 to 80 BPM and ask three friends how calm it feels, tempo is independent, calmness is dependent, and the sounds and volume stay controlled.

This is the heart of a fair test. It works for beats, for plants, for medicine, for bridges. It is how Jada tested her beat: the same class, the same time of day, the same reading time, with and without the beat. Only one thing changed.

words.d: the one thing you change on purpose in a test
what you measure to see the effect of the change
something kept the same so the test is fair

look.title: Which Change Helped?
look.text: Sam changes his beat from 110 to 90 BPM, removes the snare and turns the volume down, all at once. His friends say it is much calmer now.
look.prompt: Can Sam say which change made it calmer? Plan a better test with only one change.

check.q: Why change only one thing at a time?
choices: So you know which change caused the result
Because machines allow only one change
check.why: One change at a time links the cause to the effect.

check.q: You change the tempo and measure how calm listeners feel. What is the tempo?
check.why: The tempo is what you changed on purpose.

check.q: In Jada's test, what was a controlled variable?
choices: The time of day the class heard it
How long the class took to settle
check.why: She kept the time of day the same so the test was fair.

lessons.title: Reading a Waveform
lessons.mainIdea: On an oscilloscope, you can read a sound's loudness from the height of the waves and its pitch from how close they are.
reading: Play your beat into the Oscilloscope. The line jumps each time a drum hits and settles back between hits. The picture is the beat's *waveform*. Reading it is like reading a graph: time runs left to right, and the height of the line shows the push and pull of the air.

Look for three things. First, how tall do the biggest waves get? That is the peak amplitude, the loudest moment. If the waves hit the top of the screen and flatten, the sound is *clipping*, too loud for the system, and it will sound harsh. Second, how quickly does each hit fade? That is its *decay*. Third, how far apart are the hits? That is the rhythm.

You can adjust the screen. Stretching the time scale lets you zoom in on one kick to see its individual wiggles. Squeezing it lets you see a whole bar. Changing the height scale lets you see quiet sounds. A good scientist chooses the scale that shows what they want to measure.

words.d: the shape a sound makes when it is drawn over time
when a sound is too loud for a system and the tops of its waves get cut flat
how quickly a sound fades after it starts

look.title: Flat Tops
look.text: A student turns her beat all the way up. On the Oscilloscope, the tops and bottoms of the kick's waves are cut flat, like a mesa. The kick now sounds crackly.
look.prompt: What is happening? What should she change, and what will the waveform look like after?

check.q: On a waveform, what does the height of the biggest wave show?
check.why: Height shows amplitude, so the peak is the loudest moment.

check.q: The tops of the waves are cut flat. What is this called?
check.why: Clipping happens when a sound is too loud for the system.

check.q: To see one kick drum's wiggles up close, what do you change?
choices: Stretch the time scale to zoom in
check.why: A stretched time scale spreads out a short moment so you can see detail.

lessons.title: Kick and Hi-Hat on the Screen
lessons.mainIdea: A kick drum draws slow, big waves, and a hi-hat draws fast, small, noisy ones, which matches how low and high they sound.
reading: Play a kick drum alone into the Oscilloscope. You see a few big, rounded waves spaced far apart, and then they fade. Those far-apart waves mean a *low frequency*, often around 50 to 100 Hz for a deep kick. Big height means strong amplitude.

Now play the hi-hat alone. The line turns into a thin, jittery smear with no smooth shape. A hi-hat is made of many *high frequencies* at once, jumbled together. Scientists call a jumble of many frequencies noise, even when it sounds nice. The hi-hat also fades quickly, so its decay is short.

Put them together, and you can see why a beat works. The kick fills the low end with big, slow energy. The hi-hat fills the high end with fast, light ticks. They do not crowd each other, because they live in different frequency ranges. Mixing engineers call this giving each sound its own space.

words.d: a slow vibration that sounds deep, like a kick drum or bass
a fast vibration that sounds bright or thin, like a hi-hat
a jumble of many frequencies at once with no single pitch

look.title: Match the Picture
look.text: Screen 1 shows a thin, jittery smear that lasts a very short time. Screen 2 shows four wide, rounded waves that shrink slowly.
look.prompt: Which screen shows the kick and which shows the hi-hat? Name two clues.

check.q: What does a kick drum look like on the Oscilloscope?
choices: Big, rounded waves spaced far apart
check.why: The kick is low frequency and strong, so its waves are wide and tall.

check.q: Why does the hi-hat look jittery?
choices: It is a single low note
It is many high frequencies mixed together
check.why: The hi-hat is a noisy mix of high frequencies.

check.q: Why don't the kick and hi-hat crowd each other in a mix?
choices: They are always at different volumes
They never play at the same time
The hi-hat is not a sound
check.why: Low kick and high hi-hat fill separate parts of the frequency range.

lessons.title: Timing Your Beat With Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: You can check a beat's tempo by measuring the time between hits and turning it back into BPM.
reading: Your drum machine says the tempo is 90 BPM. Is it? Scientists check. Play the beat into the Oscilloscope and measure the time from one kick to the next kick on the main beats. That is the beat's *period*.

Turn the period back into tempo: BPM equals 60 divided by the period in seconds. If the kicks are 0.67 seconds apart, 60 divided by 0.67 is about 90. The measurement agrees with the setting. If you measure 0.60 seconds instead, the tempo is really 100 BPM, and something is set differently than you thought.

You can also check the steps. At 90 BPM, each of the 16 steps should last about 0.167 seconds. With swing on, the pairs of steps will not be equal; the first one will be longer. Measuring lets you see swing as numbers, not just a feeling. Record your measurements in a *data table*, with the setting in one column and the measured value in the next.

words.d: the time it takes for one full wave or one beat to pass
a chart with rows and columns for recording measurements

look.title: Measured Time Between Kicks
look.cite: Expected values worked out as 60 divided by BPM, rounded
look.prompt: Work out the BPM from each period. Do they match the settings? What would you measure at 75 BPM?

check.q: Kicks are 0.5 seconds apart. What is the tempo?
check.why: 60 divided by 0.5 is 120 BPM.

check.q: What is the rule for turning a period into BPM?
choices: BPM equals 60 divided by the period in seconds
BPM equals 16 divided by the period
check.why: There are 60 seconds in a minute, so divide 60 by the seconds per beat.

check.q: With swing on, what would you measure for a pair of steps?
choices: The first step is longer than the second
check.why: Swing stretches the first step of each pair.

lessons.title: Protect Your Hearing While You Create
lessons.mainIdea: When you make music, keep volume moderate, take breaks and check your levels so your ears last a lifetime.
reading: Making beats can mean hours in headphones. That is exactly when hearing damage can sneak up, because it does not hurt. Keep the volume at a comfortable level. A good check: if someone an arm's length away has to shout for you to hear them, it is too loud.

Take *listening breaks*. Every hour or so, take off the headphones for a few minutes. Your ears get tired, and tired ears hear less detail. After a break, you will often notice things in your beat you missed. Producers call these fresh ears.

Everyone's comfort level is different. Some people find certain sounds, like sharp hi-hats or sudden crashes, painful or overwhelming. That is useful information for a designer. It is fine to turn those sounds down, choose softer ones, or wear ear defenders. A beat that works for more people is a better design.

words.d: time away from headphones or loud sound so the ears can rest
how loud a sound is set to play

look.title: The Arm's-Length Check
look.text: Leo wears headphones while making a beat. His friend stands an arm's length away and talks in a normal voice. Leo does not hear him at all.
look.prompt: What does this tell Leo? What two things should he do?

check.q: Why can hearing damage from headphones be hard to notice?
choices: It always happens in one second
check.why: Noise damage often happens without pain, so habits matter.

check.q: What are fresh ears?
choices: Rested ears that notice more after a break
check.why: After a listening break you hear more detail.

check.q: A classmate finds sharp hi-hats painful. What is a good design choice?
choices: Make them louder so they get used to it
Turn them down or use softer sounds
check.why: Designing for more people's comfort is better design.

lessons.title: Samples, Credit and Fairness
lessons.mainIdea: When you use a sound someone else made, give them credit and follow the rules for using their work.
reading: A *sample* can mean a single measurement, but in music it also means a piece of another recording used in a new song. Hip hop was built on samples: a drum break from a funk record, a horn line from a jazz record, looped and flipped into something new.

The sounds in those old records were made by real people: drummers, singers, engineers. Their work is protected by *copyright*, a law that gives creators rights over how their work is used. Professional musicians who sample a song usually ask permission and often pay the people who made it. This is called clearing a sample.

For school projects, you can use the sounds built into the Drum Machine, record your own sounds, or use sounds that are marked free to use. Either way, give *credit*: write down where each sound came from. Scientists do the same when they cite other people's data. Credit is how we show respect for the work we build on.

words.d: in music, a piece of a recording reused in a new piece
a law that gives creators rights over how their work is copied and used
saying clearly who made something or where it came from

look.title: The Borrowed Horn
look.text: A student loops a horn part from a famous song in his beat. He posts it online. Someone asks who played the horn part.
look.prompt: What should the student have done before posting? How is this like a scientist citing data?

check.q: What is a music sample?
choices: A free trial of an app
A piece of a recording reused in a new piece
check.why: In music, a sample is borrowed from another recording.

check.q: What does copyright protect?
choices: A creator's rights over how their work is used
check.why: Copyright gives creators rights over copying and use.

check.q: How are giving credit in music and in science alike?
choices: Both show where the work you built on came from
check.why: Credit, in music or science, names the source.

lessons.title: Explain Your Beat Like a Scientist
lessons.mainIdea: A strong explanation makes a claim, backs it with measured evidence and uses science to explain why.
reading: You designed a beat. You measured it. Now share it the way scientists share their work: with a *claim*, *evidence* and *reasoning*. The claim is one sentence saying what your beat does. For example: my beat helps our class settle faster after lunch.

The evidence is what you measured. Jada's class took an average of about 6 minutes to settle without the beat and about 4 minutes with it, over one week each. Her oscilloscope showed no clipping and a steady 70 BPM. Evidence is numbers and observations, not just feelings, though listeners' comments count as evidence too if you collect them fairly.

The reasoning explains why the evidence supports the claim, using science. A steady pulse is easy for the brain to predict. A slow tempo is near a resting heart rate. No sudden loud sounds means nothing startles. Honest scientists also say what they are not sure of: one class, two weeks, and other things might have changed too.

words.d: a one-sentence statement that answers a question
measurements and observations that support a claim
the science that explains why the evidence supports the claim

look.title: Weak or Strong?
look.text: Explanation A: My beat is calm because it just is and I like it. Explanation B: My beat is calm. It runs at 70 BPM, has no sudden sounds and never clips on the Oscilloscope. Five of six listeners rated it calm. A slow, steady pulse is easy to predict.
look.prompt: Which explanation is stronger? Point to the claim, the evidence and the reasoning.

check.q: What is the evidence in a scientific explanation?
check.why: Evidence is what you measured and observed.

check.q: Which is a claim?
choices: Five of six listeners rated it calm
My beat helps our class settle faster
Steady pulses are easy to predict
check.why: A claim answers the question in one sentence. The others are evidence or reasoning.

check.q: Why should Jada mention it was only one class for two weeks?
choices: To make the beat sound better
Honest scientists name the limits of their evidence
check.why: Naming limits helps others judge how strong the evidence is.

review.q: What are criteria in design?
choices: The things a design must do to succeed
The limits you must work within
The sounds in a drum machine
review.why: Criteria define success; constraints are the limits.

review.q: Why build a beat in layers?
choices: To hear what each part adds
review.why: One layer at a time shows each part's effect.

review.q: You change only the tempo and measure how calm listeners feel. What is calmness?
review.why: Calmness is what you measure in response.

review.q: The tops of a waveform are cut flat. What should you do?
review.why: Flat tops mean clipping. Lowering the level fixes it.

review.q: Which sound draws big, slow, rounded waves?
review.why: The kick is low frequency and strong.

review.q: Kicks on the main beats are 1.0 second apart. What is the tempo?
review.why: 60 divided by 1.0 is 60 BPM.

review.q: Which is a good hearing habit while making beats?
choices: Keep the volume at the maximum
review.why: Breaks rest the ears and give fresh ears.

review.q: What should you do when you use someone else's sound?
choices: Change its tempo so no one knows
Give credit and follow the rules for using it
review.why: Credit and permission respect the creator's work.
